Series::AntidiffAccessor API Reference¶

Back to Series API Reference

This page is the landing page for the antiderivative workflow entered through Series::antidiff and continued through Series::AntidiffAccessor. The accessor groups sampled-data antidifferentiation methods — composite-trapezoidal integration and its running form — under one namespace, the same way linearalg groups vector/matrix methods and stat groups descriptive statistics.

Using This Reference¶

  • Use the method rail to open one accessor method at a time.

  • Each method page owns its signatures, shape contract, gradient model, verified examples, failures, and previous/next navigation.

  • Start at Series::antidiff when you need the accessor calling model; start here when you already know which operation you need.

Read This First¶

The accessor supports three equivalent-in-spirit calling styles:

auto area1 = y.antidiff.trapezoid(x);      // dot-style, x passed directly
auto area2 = y.antidiff(x).trapezoid();    // proxy style, x bound first
auto area3 = y.antidiff.trapezoid(0.5);    // dx-only, no x Series at all

The first two integrate y against explicit x-coordinates and always agree. The third needs no x-coordinates — a uniform spacing dx is enough, and it defaults to 1.0 when omitted entirely (y.antidiff.trapezoid()).

antidiff is named for what it reverses: Series::diff(), the discrete forward difference. Both operate on an already-materialized sequence of numbers. It is deliberately not the accessor for integrating an arbitrary function — that is pluss::subsp::math::integ::quadra/aleatoria/Analytica (PlussMa), which need to re-invoke a callable at points they choose, not read off values a Series already holds. See Series::antidiff for the full distinction.

Method Pages¶

  • trapezoid: total area under y over x (or a uniform spacing), reduced along one dimension — torch parity with torch.trapezoid

  • cumulative_trapezoid: the running antiderivative, one value per sample point — torch parity with torch.cumulative_trapezoid

  • ito, strat, theta: stochastic integrals of an integrand that is already sampled, against a sampled path

  • quadratic_variation, covariation: sums of squared and cross increments of sampled paths

The handwritten reference covers the complete Series::AntidiffAccessor surface.

Choosing Between Them¶

Use trapezoid() when only the total area is needed — a single number (or one number per batch row, see below). Use cumulative_trapezoid() when the running antiderivative itself is needed at every sample point, not just its final value; cumulative_trapezoid()’s last entry always equals trapezoid()’s result computed over the same data, since the total area is the running sum’s final term.

Batching¶

Both methods reduce (or accumulate) along one dimension only (dim, default the last axis). Any number of leading axes are treated as independent batch rows sharing the same x-coordinates, so one call prices an entire batch — a whole strike/maturity grid, or many independent Monte Carlo paths — without a per-row loop.

Example¶

auto y = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0}, {2, 4});
auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0});

std::cout << y.antidiff.trapezoid(x, -1) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[7.5, 75]

Two independent rows, one shared x, one call.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • antidiff is an accessor, not a materialized result.

  • The zero-argument dot-style form silently falls back to dx = 1.0 unless a peer was bound via y.antidiff(x) first — this is a legitimate calling form, not a missing-argument error.

  • x (when supplied) must be broadcastable against y along the reduced dimension; a genuinely incompatible length throws.

  • Both methods are built entirely from ordinary differentiable Series primitives (diff, slice, mul, add, sum/cumsum), so gradients flow through them for free — no custom backward rule exists for either.
